newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Troubled Ukraine farms need more than new minister.
newsitem.headline: Troubled Ukraine farms need more than new minister.

text.p: Ukrainian President Leonid Kuchma's move to expand the brief of the official in charge of farming and agriculture was dismissed as meaningless by Western experts on Tuesday.
Mykhailo Zubets, deputy prime minister in charge of agriculture, was also named agriculture minister, replacing Anatoly Khorishko who was fired by Kuchma in February for incompetence.

"Zubets is already vice prime minister for the whole complex, so he's already calling the shots," said one farming specialist, who said the performance of the agricultural sector had not shone under Zubets.
"It would have been nice if they'd picked someone snazzy and dynamic, but even that would not have made much difference," he said.
Decisions on agriculture continued to be made by the the president or his prime minister, Pavlo Lazarenko, he added.
"This happens in any country. But all they're doing is jumbling up people over and over again," he said.
Ukraine has forecast a 38 million tonne grain harvest this year -- which analysts dubbed ambitious, considering the sector's myriad problems.
A poor crop of 25.4 million tonnes in 1996 has been blamed on severe drought.
The agriculture sector is plagued by shortages of cash needed to buy seeds, fuel, fertilisers, herbicides and machinery, resulting in steadily declining harvests since independence in 1991.
Zubets, president of the Academy of Agriculture Sciences and a scientist who specialised in livestock breeding, was appointed to the post of deputy prime minister in March 1996.
Another analyst said a major problem was Ukraine's slowness in reforming the sector to free market ways, with an entrenched bureaucracy preferring to use Soviet, state-run farming methods.
"The biggest problem affecting agriculture in this country right now is the question of how agriculture is going to be," the expert said.
"Is it going to be a free market or not? Are they going to have small farms or large ones? Are there going to be private farmers or large collectives? These issues are huge," he said.
The government has repeatedly stated that it would continue to support large collective farms.
While a small handful of private farmers have cropped up since independence, they face major hurdles in competing with the state-run sector.
